method: Geostationary look angles are solved as vectors in Earth-centred coordinates. The site sits at latitude phi and longitude lambda on a sphere of radius 6,378.137 km, and the satellite sits over the equator at longitude lambda-s on a circle of radius 42,164.17 km (35,786 km altitude). The line of sight is the satellite position minus the site position and its length is the slant range. Elevation is the angle between that vector and the local up direction (cos phi cos lambda, cos phi sin lambda, sin phi); azimuth is atan2 of the vector's projection on local east (-sin lambda, cos lambda, 0) and local north (-sin phi cos lambda, -sin phi sin lambda, cos phi), measured clockwise from true north and named on a 16-point compass. The angle at the Earth's centre between site and satellite, psi, gives the ground distance to the sub-satellite point as 6,378.137 x psi. A negative elevation means the satellite is below the horizon. Latitude is limited to -90 to 90 degrees and both longitudes to -180 to 180; blank, non-numeric and out-of-range values are rejected with an actionable message. The Earth is modelled as a sphere and the orbit as perfectly equatorial and geostationary, so elevation can differ by up to about 0.2 degrees from an ellipsoidal solution at high latitude; terrain, buildings, the satellite footprint edge, rain fade and dish pointing error are not modelled. Azimuth is true, not magnetic. The calculation runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: Geostationary orbit: 35,786 km above the equator, 42,164.17 km from the Earth centre, fixed longitude
Look-angle geometry: elevation from the line-of-sight vector against local up, azimuth clockwise from true north, sub-satellite ground distance from the central angle
WGS 84 equatorial radius 6,378.137 km used for the spherical site model
